justification_text:
My point estimates reflected a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, the estimate of 109.8 was anchored closely to the last observed price, with only a small expected move given typical daily volatility and no immediate catalyst suggesting a sharp directional break. For the one-week estimate of 110.5, I incorporated a slight positive drift assumption, consistent with a mild bullish trend or mean-reverting tendency around a short-term support level. The one-month estimate of 112.0 extended that drift further, reflecting the compounding of small expected daily gains while acknowledging that over longer horizons the central tendency becomes less reliable and more dependent on fundamental or macro assumptions.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, a 90% CI of roughly plus or minus 3.3 points is consistent with typical realized volatility for a moderately volatile asset — perhaps annualized volatility in the range of 20–30%, translated into a daily standard deviation. By one week, the interval widens to plus or minus 6.5 points, reflecting the square-root-of-time scaling of volatility as well as the increased probability of a regime shift or news event over five trading days. The one-month interval of plus or minus 14 points is substantially wider, accounting for the real possibility that trend assumptions break down, macro conditions shift, or sentiment reverses meaningfully over a four-week window.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic data surprises such as an unexpected inflation print, central bank policy shifts, or geopolitical shocks that cause broad repricing across asset classes. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings release, a positive policy announcement, or a short squeeze could drive the price well above 126 at the one-month horizon. On the downside, a risk-off episode, liquidity crisis, or sector-specific bad news could easily break through the lower bound of 98.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively continuous price behavior and do not fully account for gap risk — situations where the asset opens substantially higher or lower due to overnight news. Such gaps are by definition hard to capture in any probabilistic framework built on historical volatility alone, and they represent the primary reason why real-world tail outcomes can exceed even 90% confidence bounds more frequently than the stated 10% probability would suggest.
